h1: Registering a steam boiler for a brewhouse in India
title: Registering a Brewhouse Steam Boiler | Craft Beer School
desc: The process for registering a steam boiler at an Indian brewery: what the boiler laws cover, the usual steps, documents, inspections and the plan to follow.
teaser: The boiler is the one piece of kit that has its own law. Skip the paperwork and an inspector can stop the brewhouse.
standfirst: Many brewhouses in India run on steam. Steam boilers are regulated separately from the brewery licence. Here is the usual route from choosing a boiler to running it legally, at process level. Rules differ by state and change.
sections: Why a boiler is its own regulated item

Steam under pressure stores a great deal of energy. A boiler failure can kill. For that reason India has long regulated boilers under a national Boilers Act, with regulations on design, materials, testing and inspection. The states administer it through an office usually called the Boiler Inspectorate or Directorate of Boilers.

This is separate from your excise licence and from your factory or fire approvals. A brewery can hold a valid alcohol licence and still be breaking the law if its boiler is not registered and inspected. Treat the boiler as its own project with its own timeline.

We are not lawyers or inspectors. The points below describe the usual process so you know what to ask. Confirm every step with your state boiler office or a consultant before you spend money.
Check whether your unit counts as a boiler

The law defines a boiler by what it does and its size. Very small steam generators can fall below the legal threshold, while an ordinary brewhouse steam unit usually sits above it. The definition and the limits are in the law and have changed before. Do not rely on a supplier saying "it does not need registration". Ask the boiler office in writing, or have a consultant do it.

If you are weighing heating options, our guide to steam versus electric heating for a brewpub brewhouse compares the running side. This guide covers the paperwork if you choose steam.

The sequence tends to look like this. Names and forms vary by state.

  1. Choose a manufacturer approved under the boiler regulations. An unapproved maker's boiler cannot normally be registered.
  2. Get the design drawings and calculations approved by the state boiler authority before manufacture.
  3. Have the boiler inspected and tested during manufacture, including a hydraulic pressure test, by an authorised inspecting authority.
  4. Receive the manufacturer's certificates and test records.
  5. Submit an application for registration to the state boiler office, with the documents they ask for.
  6. Have the installation inspected on site before first use.
  7. Receive a registration number and a certificate to operate, which you must renew on time.

Do not fire the boiler for production until the certificate is in hand. A test run before approval is a common mistake.

Ask your boiler office for the exact list. You can expect to need:

  • The manufacturer's approval and the design drawings.
  • Material and test certificates for pressure parts.
  • Records of the hydraulic test.
  • Layout drawings of the boiler room and the steam piping.
  • Proof of ownership and the site address.
  • Details of the person who will operate the boiler.

Keep scans and the originals in a single file. The inspector can ask for any of them years later.

Many states require a qualified person to operate or supervise a boiler. The requirement depends on the size and type. Check it before you hire. A brewery that depends on one certified person has a gap whenever that person is on leave.

The fuel matters too. Diesel, gas, biomass and electric boilers have different storage and flue rules. A brewhouse in a shared building also has to think about where steam and flue gases go, which our guide to kitchen exhaust and brewhouse steam vents in a shared building covers.

The boiler room itself needs space for inspection, ventilation, a safe distance from drains and tanks and a clear escape route. Plan that at the layout stage, not after the boiler arrives.
A second hand boiler is a bigger question

A used boiler has its own history. It may have been registered in another state, its records may be incomplete and its remaining life may be short. Many boiler offices want to re-inspect it and re-test the pressure parts before they will register it to a new owner. Treat that as part of the price. Our guide to buying a second hand brewhouse in India and what to inspect sets out what else to check.

Registration is not the end. The boiler needs periodic inspection, usually yearly. The certificate has to be renewed before it lapses. Keep a log of daily checks: water level, safety valves, pressure gauge, blowdown and feed water treatment. Poor feed water scales the tubes and cuts efficiency long before it causes a failure.

Put the renewal dates in the same calendar as your excise and licence dates. A lapsed certificate can stop production at the worst moment. Costs for fees, inspection and operator wages belong in your plan as well. Our course on brewery business management shows how to carry them into a cost per litre.
faqs: Does a brewery steam boiler need to be registered in India?
A boiler above the legal size limit normally does. National boiler law and state rules decide, so confirm with your state boiler office whether your unit counts.
Is boiler registration part of the excise licence?
No. It is a separate process with a separate authority. A brewery needs both.
Can I run the boiler during commissioning before the certificate arrives?
You should not run it for production before approval. Ask the boiler office what is allowed for testing.
Do I need a certified boiler operator?
Many states require one, depending on size and type. Check the current rules before you hire.
